questions.q: According to the lesson, what is the right first step when choosing quantum hardware for a given problem?
options: Start with whichever vendor currently advertises the highest qubit count and work backward from there
Choose the platform that is cheapest per hour regardless of what the workload actually needs
Pick the platform used in the most recently published research paper, regardless of workload fit
Characterize the workload's qubit count, circuit depth, connectivity pattern, and error tolerance first, then compare platforms against those requirements
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly frames the wrong approach as starting from the vendor list/biggest number, and the right approach as characterizing the workload's real requirements first, then matching platforms to those requirements.

questions.q: Why does a shallow, many-qubit, noise-tolerant workload like a variational algorithm often favor a platform that scales qubit count well even at moderate per-gate fidelity?
options: Because variational algorithms never use any classical computation at all

Because each individual circuit run is shallow and the classical optimization loop iterating on top of it can tolerate a fair amount of per-run noise, so usable qubit count matters more than top-tier fidelity for this shape
Because shallow circuits always require the single highest fidelity available on any platform
Because qubit count has no effect on whether a variational algorithm can represent its problem
questions.explain: The lesson ties this workload shape to superconducting platforms specifically because they've historically offered more usable qubits at acceptable fidelity, which suits a noise-tolerant, iterative, shallow-circuit algorithm.

questions.q: Why does a workload requiring all-to-all connectivity (e.g., certain optimization problems or chemistry Hamiltonians) create a problem on a sparsely connected, nearest-neighbor device?
options: Because the compiler must insert heavy SWAP overhead to route non-adjacent qubit interactions, which can dominate the circuit's real depth and erode the benefit of an otherwise capable device
Because nearest-neighbor devices have no qubits capable of entangling with each other at all
Because all-to-all connectivity requirements make a circuit impossible to compile on any hardware whatsoever
Because connectivity requirements only affect classical post-processing, never the quantum circuit itself
questions.explain: This directly reuses the SWAP-overhead concept from earlier in the chapter: a mismatch between a workload's required connectivity and a device's actual topology can inflate real circuit depth well beyond what qubit count or fidelity numbers alone would suggest.

questions.q: Besides the physics of qubit count, fidelity, and connectivity, what non-technical factors does the lesson say belong in a real hardware decision?
options: The number of academic citations a hardware paper has received
Nothing -- the lesson argues only the physical specifications should ever factor into the decision
Only the color scheme of the vendor's marketing website
Cloud access and cost, queue time, SDK/toolchain maturity, and vendor roadmap/support
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly lists cloud access/cost, queue time, SDK/toolchain maturity, and vendor roadmap/support as practical factors just as real as the underlying physics when making an actual hardware choice.

questions.q: What distinguishes a defensible hardware recommendation from a weak one, according to the lesson's closing section?
options: A defensible recommendation requires no justification as long as the chosen platform is popular
A defensible recommendation is always the platform with the lowest advertised cost, regardless of fit
A defensible recommendation never mentions any tradeoffs, since admitting a tradeoff weakens the case
A defensible recommendation names the workload's requirements, the platform chosen, and what was explicitly given up to get there, rather than simply citing the platform with the most qubits
questions.explain: The lesson contrasts 'we chose X because fidelity mattered more here, accepting a longer queue and fewer qubits' (a real decision) against 'we chose the platform with the most qubits' (no decision at all, just the 'biggest number wins' thinking the chapter has been debunking).
